prompt.context: Your friend owns a single mom-and-pop supermarket. He has noticed that his supermarket competitors have added pharmacies and is wondering whether or not he should do the same. He has data sources and can provide information you request, but first needs to know what data you need to make this decision. Because this is a small operation, he needs a payback period of less than 2 years (no discounting necessary).
prompt.question: Should your friend add a pharmacy to his grocery store? What data would you need, and is the investment justified given a payback requirement of under 2 years?

clarifying_info.q: How many unique customers does the store have each month?
What percentage of the population has prescriptions?
clarifying_info.a: On average, 50% of the population have prescriptions, averaging 1 filling per month.
There are 2 pharmacies and 2 grocery stores within 4 miles of his store.

clarifying_info.q: How much does each customer currently spend at the store?
clarifying_info.a: Each customer spends $100 per month (assume 1 visit per month).

clarifying_info.q: What revenue does a prescription sale generate?
clarifying_info.a: Each prescription sale brings in revenue of $50.

clarifying_info.q: Do pharmacy customers change their grocery shopping behavior?
clarifying_info.a: Each prescription customer tends to spend 30% more on groceries at the store.

clarifying_info.q: What is the initial investment required?
clarifying_info.a: The initial investment for the pharmacy is $1.2 million.
For the pharmacy, assume costs are equal to 90% of revenue.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current grocery cost structure?

framework: Define investment criteria: payback < 2 years, no discounting
Estimate addressable market: current customers, town population, pharmacy market size
Estimate revenue from pharmacy: prescription revenue + incremental grocery revenue
Estimate costs: pharmacy operating costs (90% of revenue) and initial capex
Calculate break-even number of pharmacy customers and assess feasibility
Benchmark against competitive landscape and make recommendation

questions.prompt: What is the population of the town and the addressable pharmacy market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate market share of existing grocery business (~33%), back into total unique customers in town, multiply by household size to get population, then apply the 50% prescription rate.

math.setup: Assume grocery market share is 33%; 10,000 customers / 0.33 = total unique grocery customers in town. Multiply by ~3 people per household for population. Apply 50% prescription rate for pharmacy market.
steps: 30,000 * 3 people/household = ~100,000 population (casebook rounds to 33,000 customers -> 100,000 population using 10,000/0.33=33,000)
math.answer: Town population ~100,000; addressable pharmacy market ~50,000 customers.

questions.prompt: Of the grocer's 10,000 existing customers, how many have prescription needs?
questions.guidance: Use probability: at least 1 person per household has prescription needs. With 3 people per household each having 50% probability, use complement rule.

math.setup: Probability that at least 1 person in a 3-person household needs a prescription = 1 - P(none need prescription) = 1 - (0.5)^3.
steps: 10,000 current customers * 87.5% = 8,750 customers with prescription needs
math.answer: ~8,750 of the grocer's current 10,000 customers have prescription needs.

questions.prompt: What is the incremental annual value of a pharmacy customer?
questions.guidance: Combine margin from prescription drug sales with the incremental grocery margin from the 30% uplift in spending. Candidate must calculate margins, not just revenue.

math.setup: Prescription revenue per customer per month = $50; pharmacy cost = 90% of revenue, so margin = 10% => $5/month. Incremental grocery spend = $100 * 30% = $30/month at 50% gross margin (100% - 70% COGS) = $15/month. Total incremental margin per pharmacy customer per month = $5 + $15 = $20.
steps: Drug margin per customer per month: $50 * 10% = $5
Grocery gross margin: 100% - 70% COGS = 30%; but casebook uses 50% margin on incremental -> $30 * 50% = $15
Annual incremental value: $20 * 12 = $240 per pharmacy customer per year
math.answer: $240 per pharmacy customer per year; $480 over 2 years.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum market share needed to break even in 2 years? Is this reasonable?
questions.guidance: Divide the $1.2M investment by the 2-year value per customer. Compare to the pool of 8,750 existing customers with prescription needs to assess feasibility.

math.setup: Break-even customers needed = Initial investment / 2-year value per customer. Then compare to existing customer pool with prescription needs.
steps: 2,500 / 8,750 = ~28.6%, or roughly 30% of existing customers with prescription needs
Only need ~30% of current customers who already have prescriptions to switch to fill them at the new pharmacy
math.answer: Need 2,500 pharmacy customers; that is only ~30% of the 8,750 existing customers who have prescription needs — a very achievable target.

questions.prompt: What are the two major cost categories when opening a pharmacy?
questions.guidance: Capital expenditure (initial investment) and ongoing operating costs (pharmacist labor, drugs/COGS, regulatory compliance). The case simplifies ongoing costs to 90% of revenue.

steps: Ongoing operating costs: 90% of pharmacy revenue (covers pharmacist labor, drug COGS, compliance, etc.)
math.answer: Capital investment ($1.2M) and operating costs (90% of pharmacy revenue).

brainstorming.prompt: What next steps should your friend take if he decides to proceed with opening the pharmacy?

categories.name: Design & Construction
ideas: Commission design plans for the pharmacy space
Build out pharmacy counter and storage

categories.name: Financing
ideas: Secure a bank loan to fund the $1.2M investment
Explore SBA or small business financing options

categories.name: Staffing
ideas: Train existing store staff on pharmacy customer service

categories.name: Supply Chain
ideas: Contact drug reps and determine suppliers
Negotiate supplier contracts for drug inventory

categories.name: Marketing
ideas: Market the new pharmacy service to existing 10,000 customers
Launch loyalty program integrating grocery and pharmacy

categories.name: Competitive Strategy
ideas: Consider approaching existing drug-store competitors about a JV or partnership
Monitor competitor response (2 pharmacies within 4 miles may retaliate)
Differentiate on convenience and personal service vs. chain pharmacies

recommendation: Proceed with adding the pharmacy. The investment is highly likely to pay back within 2 years.
Only ~30% capture of existing customers with prescription needs (2,500 out of 8,750) is sufficient to break even — a conservative and achievable threshold.
The dual revenue uplift (pharmacy margin + increased grocery spend) makes the economics compelling.
risks: Competitive retaliation from the 2 existing pharmacies and 2 grocery stores nearby
Regulatory and licensing complexity for a first-time pharmacy operator
Execution risk: hiring qualified pharmacists and managing drug inventory
Lower-than-expected capture rate if customers are loyal to existing pharmacies
next_steps: Make design plans and obtain required pharmacy licenses/permits
Market the new service to existing customer base
Contact drug suppliers and establish inventory system
Assess whether a JV with an existing local pharmacy could reduce execution risk
